generic: Chromium (Trivalent chromium - e.g., chromium picolinate/chloride; as supplement and in parenteral nutrition)
pharm: Trivalent chromium is an essential trace element thought to potentiate insulin action and support normal carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism; supplied as a dietary supplement and as a trace element in parenteral nutrition.
quick: Oral supplement commonly 200 mcg/day (up to ~1000 mcg in studies); PN typically 10-15 mcg/day
Oral chromium is often taken with food
Adequate intake ~30 mcg/day; avoid high-dose supplements
Adequate intake ~45 mcg/day; avoid high-dose supplements
Reduce/omit parenteral chromium in renal impairment (accumulation)
Caution; chromium is excreted renally, monitor in PN
Blood glucose in diabetics; renal function for parenteral use
summary: Chromium (in its trivalent form) is an essential trace element involved in normal carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism and is believed to enhance the action of insulin. It is used as an oral dietary supplement (commonly chromium picolinate or chloride) and as a trace-element additive in parenteral nutrition to prevent or correct deficiency. Trivalent chromium has low oral toxicity; very high doses have rarely been associated with kidney or liver effects. It should be distinguished from hexavalent chromium, which is toxic and carcinogenic and is not used therapeutically. People with diabetes on supplements should monitor blood glucose, as chromium may modestly affect it.
indications: Prevention and treatment of chromium deficiency, including as a trace-element component of parenteral (intravenous) nutrition
Dietary supplementation to maintain adequate chromium intake (oral)

dosage.d: Commonly 50-200 mcg daily (trivalent chromium); some studies use up to ~1000 mcg/day
dosage.n: No established RDA; adequate intake ~20-35 mcg/day

dosage.d: Approximately 10-15 mcg daily added to the PN admixture

dosage.c: Parenteral nutrition - increased needs (e.g., intestinal losses)

admin: Oral supplements: take with or after food; follow the product label
Parenteral chromium is a concentrated additive that must be diluted into the parenteral nutrition admixture before infusion - never give the concentrate undiluted or as a direct IV push
Use aseptic technique when adding to parenteral nutrition
Adjust or omit parenteral chromium in renal impairment to avoid accumulation
Distinguish trivalent (nutritional) chromium from toxic hexavalent chromium
moa: Trivalent chromium is an essential micronutrient. It is thought to act by potentiating the action of insulin: chromium is a component of a low-molecular-weight chromium-binding substance (sometimes called chromodulin) that, when bound to chromium, enhances insulin receptor tyrosine kinase activity and downstream insulin signaling. This promotes normal glucose uptake and metabolism and supports normal lipid and protein metabolism. Adequate chromium status is required for normal carbohydrate metabolism, and deficiency (seen historically in long-term parenteral nutrition without chromium) produces impaired glucose tolerance.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to chromium or to a specific product component
relative: Significant renal impairment (risk of accumulation, especially parenteral)
Pre-existing renal or hepatic disease with high-dose oral supplementation
Diabetes on insulin/antidiabetic drugs (may affect glucose control)
monitor: Blood glucose in patients with diabetes
Renal and hepatic function during prolonged parenteral supplementation
Signs of chromium toxicity with high-dose use

preg: Adequate chromium intake in pregnancy is about 30 mcg/day, generally met by diet. High-dose chromium supplements are not recommended in pregnancy due to limited safety data; routine prenatal nutrition usually suffices.
lact: Adequate chromium intake during lactation is about 45 mcg/day. High-dose supplements are not recommended; chromium is present in breast milk in small amounts and dietary intake is generally adequate.
renal: Chromium is eliminated mainly by the kidneys. In renal impairment, parenteral chromium can accumulate; reduce the dose or omit it from parenteral nutrition and monitor as appropriate.
hepatic: Use caution with parenteral chromium in hepatic dysfunction. Very high oral doses have rarely been linked to hepatic effects; monitor liver function with prolonged high-dose supplementation.

moderate: Antidiabetic drugs (insulin, sulfonylureas, metformin) - chromium may enhance glucose lowering; monitor blood glucose
Levothyroxine - chromium (e.g., picolinate) may reduce thyroid hormone absorption; separate dosing
minor: Antacids, calcium carbonate, and other minerals - may reduce chromium absorption
interactions.food: Foods high in simple sugars may increase chromium excretion; vitamin C may enhance absorption. Oral chromium is often taken with food.
interactions.diagnostics: High-dose supplementation may lower blood glucose readings; serum/urine chromium can be measured to assess status.

common: Generally well tolerated at usual doses
serious: Renal impairment with very high doses (rare)
rare: Rhabdomyolysis (rare reports with very high-dose chromium picolinate)
Mood changes/cognitive effects (rare reports at high doses)
emergency: Acute kidney injury or hepatic injury from massive overdose
Severe hypoglycemia in combination with antidiabetic drugs

monitoring: Blood glucose in patients with diabetes or on antidiabetic therapy
Renal and hepatic function during prolonged parenteral nutrition or high-dose oral use
Clinical signs of deficiency (impaired glucose tolerance, peripheral neuropathy) in long-term PN
Serum/urine chromium where assessment of status is needed
counsel: Chromium is an essential trace mineral; usual supplement doses are generally safe
If you have diabetes, monitor your blood sugar, as chromium may lower it - report unusual low blood sugar
Take separately from antacids, calcium, and thyroid medication, which can affect absorption
Do not take very high doses; more is not better and may rarely affect the kidneys or liver
Tell your clinician about all supplements and medicines you take
pk: Acts as a nutrient; metabolic effects develop gradually with adequate intake
Oral absorption is low (roughly 0.4-2.5% of trivalent chromium absorbed)
Tissue retention is variable; absorbed chromium is excreted in urine over days
Store oral supplements in a cool, dry place; store parenteral additive per the product label
pearls: Only trivalent chromium is nutritional; hexavalent chromium is toxic/carcinogenic and is not used therapeutically
Oral absorption is low (about 0.4-2.5%); it is a supplement rather than an FDA-approved drug, while injectable trace-element chromium is an Rx parenteral nutrition additive
May modestly potentiate insulin - patients with diabetes should monitor blood glucose for hypoglycemia
Reduce or omit parenteral chromium in renal impairment because it is renally excreted and can accumulate
Separate from antacids, calcium, and levothyroxine to avoid reduced absorption
missed: For oral supplements, if you miss a dose, take it when you remember; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and resume your usual schedule. Do not double the dose. Parenteral chromium is given as part of daily nutrition by clinicians.
overdose: Acute overdose of trivalent chromium is uncommon because oral absorption is low; very large doses may cause gastrointestinal upset and, rarely, kidney or liver injury. Manage with supportive care, hydration, and monitoring of renal and hepatic function. (Hexavalent chromium poisoning is a separate, serious toxicologic emergency and is not relevant to nutritional chromium use.)
